Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a nationwide system of sortition—random lottery selection of legislative and executive leaders—instead of using traditional elections, focusing on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.
Model Response:

The Case for Sortition: Arguments and Analysis

Sortition — selecting officials by random lottery — is one of the oldest democratic ideas, used extensively in ancient Athens. It has experienced a revival in political philosophy, with serious thinkers arguing it offers genuine advantages over electoral systems. Here are the core arguments.

1. Reducing Elite Capture

The problem elections solve imperfectly: Elections require money, name recognition, media access, and professional organization. These requirements systematically favor those with wealth, connections, or institutional backing.

The sortition argument: Random selection from the full adult population would produce a legislature that mirrors the population's actual socioeconomic composition — roughly proportional representation of income levels, education backgrounds, occupations, and geographic origins — without anyone needing to fundraise, campaign, or build a political machine.

Think of it this way: if you wanted to know what your community genuinely thinks, would you ask the five people who volunteered to campaign hardest for the microphone, or would you randomly select a representative sample? The argument is that elections select for ambition and resources, not representativeness.

2. Eliminating Structural Incentives for Corruption

The electoral incentive problem: Elected officials need to win re-election. This creates structural dependencies — on donors, on party organizations, on media coverage — that shape behavior regardless of personal character. Even well-intentioned officials must allocate significant time to fundraising and political positioning.

The sortition argument: Randomly selected officials serve a single term with no re-election possibility. This eliminates the incentive to:

  • Favor donors or future employers
  • Make short-term decisions aimed at the next campaign cycle
  • Prioritize party loyalty over constituent interests
  • Engage in performative politics for media attention

A sortition-selected body, the argument goes, would have structural incentives closer to a jury — serve your term, deliberate honestly, and return to private life.

3. Genuine Descriptive Representation

The representation gap: Consider how well your national legislature matches your country's demographics by age, gender, income, education, race, profession, and religion. In most electoral systems, the gap is substantial. Legislatures tend to be wealthier, more educated, more male, older, and more legally-trained than the populations they represent.

The sortition argument: A randomly selected body would, by the mathematics of probability, achieve near-perfect descriptive representation across every dimension simultaneously — something no electoral system has ever accomplished. This matters because people with different life experiences bring different concerns, knowledge, and priorities to policy deliberation.

If the legislature needs to make decisions about agricultural policy, having actual farmers present matters. If it needs to consider healthcare, having nurses and patients present matters. Sortition would guarantee this kind of experiential diversity.

4. Reducing Partisan Polarization

The polarization feedback loop: Electoral competition incentivizes politicians to emphasize differences, mobilize base voters through fear and outrage, and treat compromise as weakness. Parties have structural incentives to polarize because moderate positions are less motivating for voter turnout.

The sortition argument: Without parties competing for seats, the incentive structure shifts dramatically. A randomly selected assembly has no campaign to win, no base to mobilize, and no opponent to demonize. Deliberation becomes the primary activity rather than positioning. Historical and contemporary examples of sortition-based bodies (citizens' assemblies in Ireland, France, Canada, and elsewhere) have shown notably civil, deliberative dynamics — participants often report shifting their views through discussion rather than entrenching them.

5. Opening Genuine Access to Power

The gatekeeping problem: In electoral systems, the pool of viable candidates is filtered through countless gatekeepers — party officials, primary voters, major donors, media editors, debate commission organizers. The people who clear every filter are, by definition, exceptional along dimensions that may not correlate with good governance.

The sortition argument: Every citizen becomes eligible. The schoolteacher, the small business owner, the retired construction worker, the single parent — people who would never run for office, never get past a party primary, never raise enough money — become equally likely to serve. This represents a fundamentally different theory of democratic competence: that ordinary people, given access to information and deliberative processes, can govern responsibly.

Important Counterarguments and Tensions

Any honest treatment of sortition must acknowledge the serious objections:

  • Competence concerns: Governance requires specialized knowledge. How do you ensure randomly selected officials can understand complex policy? Proponents respond with proposals for expert briefings, staff support, and deliberative processes — essentially arguing that informed amateurs with good structural incentives outperform captured professionals.

  • Accountability: If you can't vote officials out, how do you hold them accountable? Sortition advocates propose oversight bodies, transparent proceedings, and corruption penalties — but acknowledge this is a genuine design challenge.

  • Legitimacy and consent: Electoral systems, for all their flaws, involve active consent from the governed. Whether citizens would accept randomly selected leaders is an empirical and cultural question without a clear answer.

  • Scale and implementation: Designing a workable national system is enormously complex. Most serious proposals suggest hybrid models — sortition for one legislative chamber alongside elected officials, or citizens' assemblies with specific mandates rather than full governance replacement.

Honest Assessment

Sortition addresses real, documented failures of electoral systems — elite dominance, corruption incentives, demographic distortion, and polarization. The theoretical case is stronger than most people initially expect, and the growing body of citizens' assembly experience provides some practical evidence.

That said, no modern nation has attempted full-scale sortition governance. The idea remains largely experimental, and the transition risks from established systems are substantial. The most productive conversation is probably not "sortition versus elections" but "how might sortition complement or reform existing systems to address specific dysfunctions?"

  2. Which district lines were drawn by the party that won last time
  3. The algorithmic whims of a handful of social media platforms

"But random selection wouldn't produce qualified leaders!"

A Republic By Lot: Taking Democracy Seriously

A Speech Advocating for Sortition in the United States

My fellow citizens,

I stand before you today to make what many will call a radical proposal. But I ask you to consider that the most radical thing we can do is to finally — finally — take democracy at its word.

For nearly 250 years, we have called ourselves a democracy while operating a system that produces anything but democratic outcomes. We have elections — sacred, expensive, exhausting elections — and we have convinced ourselves that the ritual itself is the democracy. But I ask you: look at the results. Look at who actually serves. Look at who actually decides. And tell me honestly whether this system delivers what it promises.

It does not.

I am proposing that we abolish elections for legislative and executive offices and replace them with sortition — the random selection of citizens from the general population to serve in public office.

I know what you're thinking. Random? Random selection? Isn't that reckless? Isn't that handing power to chance?

But consider: we already use random selection for the most consequential single decisions any citizen can make. We trust juries — randomly selected ordinary people — to decide guilt and innocence, to send people to prison, to even determine whether someone lives or dies. We do this because we understand that a cross-section of ordinary citizens, given access to information and the space to deliberate, will render fairer judgments than any appointed panel of elites.

What is a legislature, if not a jury on the great questions of law and policy?

What is an executive, if not a citizen trusted to administer the common good?

If we trust random citizens with the power of life and death, why do we recoil at trusting them with tax rates and infrastructure bills?

The first argument for sortition is fairness.

Look at the United States Congress. Roughly half are millionaires. The median net worth of a senator exceeds $3 million. They are disproportionately lawyers and business owners. They are overwhelmingly white, overwhelmingly male, overwhelmingly drawn from the same handful of elite universities.

This is not an accident. Elections do not select for wisdom, compassion, or good judgment. Elections select for wealth, name recognition, and the willingness to spend years fundraising from powerful interests before ever casting a single vote.

Sortition would produce a legislature that actually looks like America. Not the America of campaign donors and political operatives, but the real one — the one with nurses and truck drivers and teachers and farmers and single mothers working two jobs.

Every demographic group would be represented in exact proportion to their presence in the population. Not because we mandate it, not because we set quotas, but because random selection naturally produces a faithful cross-section of society.

That is what fairness looks like. Not the performance of fairness. The real thing.

The second argument is corruption.

I want to be direct about this. Our current system is not merely imperfect — it is structurally corrupt. I do not use that word carelessly.

When a candidate must raise $10 million to run for a House seat, and $30 million or more for the Senate, where do you suppose that money comes from? From ordinary citizens? From the nurse working a double shift? From the family trying to make rent?

No. It comes from corporations, from lobbyists, from wealthy donors who expect — and receive — access, influence, and favorable policy in return. This is not a conspiracy theory. It is the open, documented, structural reality of American politics. Studies from Princeton and Northwestern have shown that when ordinary citizens want a policy, the likelihood of it becoming law is statistically no different from zero. When economic elites and organized interest groups want a policy, the probability of adoption rises dramatically.

The problem is not that we have bad apples. The problem is that elections require candidates to become dependent on the very interests they are supposed to regulate. No amount of campaign finance reform will solve this, because the corruption is not incidental to the system — it is built into the system.

Sortition eliminates this entirely. A randomly selected citizen does not owe anything to any donor. They have no campaign to finance. They have no reelection to worry about. They serve one term, and they return to private life.

Who do you suppose such a person would serve? The people. Because there is no one else they can serve.

The third argument is empowerment.

We tell our children that in America, any citizen can grow up to lead. But we all know that is a fairy tale. The barriers to political power are enormous — financial, social, institutional. Most people never even consider running for office, not because they lack intelligence or character, but because the system is designed to exclude them.

Sortition actually empowers ordinary citizens. Not symbolically. Not in a speech. In practice. Under sortition, any citizen — literally any citizen — could be called to serve. The construction worker in Ohio. The grandmother in Georgia. The recent immigrant building a new life in Arizona. Every single person has an equal chance, an equal voice, an equal stake in the future of this country.

That is not chaos. That is the purest expression of democratic equality ever devised. And it is not new. Athenian democracy — the civilization we claim to admire, the civilization that invented democracy — used sortition for nearly all public offices. They considered elections aristocratic, because elections elevated the famous and the wealthy. They chose sortition because it elevated the ordinary citizen.

They were right.

Now, I anticipate the objections, and I want to address them honestly.

"But ordinary people aren't qualified!"

Qualified by what standard? The standard that produced the Iraq War? The standard that produced a $34 trillion national debt? The standard that produced a healthcare system that bankrupts families? The standard that produced a Congress with a 15% approval rating?

I have more faith in the collective wisdom of ordinary people than in the demonstrated performance of our so-called experts. And sortition does not mean a citizen governs alone. Selected citizens would receive training, access to expert advisors, and serve alongside a large body of fellow citizens. The deliberative process itself produces wisdom. We see this in Citizens' Assemblies around the world — randomly selected groups, given information and time, consistently produce thoughtful, balanced, and often better policy than professional politicians.

"What about the President? Surely you need someone experienced!"

Why? We have had experienced presidents who led us into disaster, and we have had inexperienced presidents who rose to the moment. The qualities we need — judgment, integrity, the ability to listen — are not exclusive to any profession or pedigree. And an executive selected by lot, supported by a randomly selected legislature and a professional civil service, would govern no worse than what we have now, and likely far better, freed as they would be from the distortions of electoral ambition.

"This would never work in a country of 330 million people."

Democracy by Lot: The Case for Replacing Elections with Sortition

American democracy rests on a powerful promise: government derives its authority from the people. Yet the electoral system increasingly fails to fulfill that promise. Political influence depends heavily on wealth, party machinery, media access, personal ambition, and the ability to survive a permanent campaign. Citizens may formally select their leaders, but they usually choose among candidates filtered by donors, partisan organizations, professional consultants, and unequal access to publicity. The result is a political class that is far less representative of the public than democracy ought to be.

The United States should replace elections with sortition: the random selection of ordinary citizens to serve in legislative and executive roles for limited terms. Selection would be conducted from a broad, representative pool, much as juries are chosen today, with safeguards for demographic balance, conflicts of interest, incapacity, and undue hardship. Those selected would receive training, expert support, fair compensation, and legal protection from coercion.

Sortition would not create perfect government; no institutional arrangement can. But it would attack three of the deepest weaknesses in American politics: corruption, destructive partisanship, and the exclusion of ordinary people.

Elections Reward Fundraising Rather Than Public Judgment

Modern elections require enormous quantities of money. Candidates need funding for advertisements, travel, staff, polling, legal assistance, digital outreach, and opposition research. Even when contributions do not amount to explicit bribery, dependence on donors shapes who can run, which issues receive attention, and whose interests officials take seriously.

Political corruption is therefore broader than exchanging cash for favors. It includes an institutional culture in which leaders spend substantial time courting affluent contributors, parties recruit candidates for fundraising ability, and lobbyists gain access unavailable to ordinary citizens. The revolving door between public office and private influence further undermines trust.

Sortition would sever this relationship at its root. A randomly selected official would not need campaign contributions, endorsements, advertising, or party approval. There would be no election to finance and no donor base to repay. Citizens would enter office because they were selected to perform a civic duty, not because they succeeded in assembling a coalition of wealthy patrons.

Corruption would still be possible, so sortition would require strict ethics rules, transparent deliberations, independent inspectors general, public financial disclosures, blind trusts where appropriate, and severe penalties for bribery. But eliminating campaigns would remove one of the largest and most socially accepted channels through which private wealth influences public power.

Sortition Would Weaken Partisan Warfare

Elections encourage officials to divide society into competing camps. Candidates gain attention by portraying opponents as dangerous, emphasizing emotional conflicts, and promising victory to one coalition over another. Primary elections often reward ideological intensity, while gerrymandered districts protect incumbents from broad public accountability but expose them to challenges from partisan extremes.

Sortition would change the incentive structure. Randomly selected citizens would not need to build political brands, appease primary voters, or generate outrage for fundraising. They could approach legislation as a practical task rather than as a continuous contest for partisan advantage.

A legislature selected by lot would also contain a more authentic variety of political views. Instead of dividing almost every question between two organized parties, members would arrive with overlapping identities and experiences: a rural nurse might be fiscally cautious but supportive of public health programs; a small-business owner might favor deregulation in one field and stronger consumer protections in another. Such combinations are common among the public but poorly represented by rigid party structures.

Without electoral incentives, disagreement would remain, as it should. Democracy does not require uniformity. But conflict could focus more often on evidence, tradeoffs, and workable compromise rather than party loyalty and electoral strategy.

Ordinary People Would Finally Govern

Elected institutions disproportionately attract lawyers, business executives, wealthy individuals, political operatives, and professional campaigners. These groups may contribute valuable expertise, but they do not reflect the full range of American life. Millions of citizens who understand schools, hospitals, factories, farms, public transportation, caregiving, housing insecurity, and low-wage work rarely hold national power.

Sortition would treat practical experience as a democratic resource. A randomly selected body could include teachers, mechanics, parents, service workers, scientists, retirees, contractors, and students. If the sample were sufficiently large and carefully designed, it could resemble the country more closely than any elected legislature ever has.

This would constitute genuine political equality. Under elections, every citizen may cast a ballot, but only a narrow and self-selected class has a realistic opportunity to exercise governmental power. Under sortition, every eligible citizen would have a meaningful chance to serve. Public office would become a temporary civic responsibility rather than a career controlled by those with unusual wealth, ambition, or connections.

Service should be well paid, jobs should be legally protected, childcare and disability accommodations should be guaranteed, and hardship exemptions should be narrowly but humanely administered. Otherwise, selection would favor people able to abandon their ordinary responsibilities. Properly supported, however, sortition could bring into government precisely the citizens now excluded from it.

Random Selection Can Produce Competent Decisions

The most common objection is that government is too complicated to entrust to randomly selected citizens. Yet elections do not test competence. Voters do not administer examinations in constitutional law, economics, public health, military strategy, or public administration. Electoral success primarily demonstrates skill in campaigning.

Sortition would separate representation from expertise. Citizens would make judgments about public goals and tradeoffs, while permanent professional institutions would supply technical knowledge. Selected officials could hear testimony from competing experts, question administrators, commission independent research, and deliberate over time. Policy staff would be assigned through nonpartisan public agencies rather than chosen by parties or lobbyists.

This resembles the jury system. Jurors are not expected to arrive as forensic experts or legal scholars. They receive evidence, hear opposing arguments, obtain instructions, deliberate, and render a judgment. The legitimacy of the process comes partly from the fact that ordinary citizens—not a permanent caste—exercise power.

The best defense against incompetence is therefore not campaigning but institutional support: extensive training, transparent evidence, balanced briefings, professional civil servants, judicial review, and collective decision-making. Large randomly selected bodies would also dilute the effect of any one member’s ignorance or extremism.

Executive Power Could Also Be Selected by Lot

Applying sortition to executive leadership would require additional safeguards because executive decisions often demand speed, coordination, and specialized management. The answer is not to preserve presidential elections but to redesign executive authority.

Rather than randomly appointing one citizen as an unchecked president, the United States could use a plural executive council selected by lot. Its members would serve staggered terms, receive intensive preparation, and make major decisions collectively. Professional administrators would operate federal departments under public mandates, while the council would set priorities, supervise implementation, and respond to emergencies.

A collective executive would reduce the risks of personality cults, demagoguery, and arbitrary rule. It would also prevent national politics from revolving around one charismatic figure. Emergency powers should be narrow, temporary, transparent, and subject to rapid review by the sortition legislature and the courts.

Sortition Would Improve Accountability

Critics may argue that elections allow voters to remove bad officials. In practice, however, electoral accountability is weak. Incumbents benefit from name recognition, donor networks, partisan loyalty, and favorable district boundaries. Voters are asked to evaluate thousands of decisions through a single ballot, often with limited information and only two viable choices.

Sortition would replace electoral accountability with legal and institutional accountability. Officials would serve short, nonrenewable terms, eliminating incentives to cling to office. Their finances and official contacts would be disclosed. Independent bodies could investigate misconduct. Recall panels selected by lot could remove officials for corruption, incapacity, or serious abuse. Courts would continue to enforce constitutional limits, and public records laws would expose decision-making to scrutiny.

Nonrenewable service is especially important. An official who cannot campaign for another term has less reason to manipulate public opinion or grant favors in exchange for political support. Power becomes temporary by design.

The Risks Are Real but Manageable

Random selection could produce unqualified, prejudiced, or irresponsible officials. But elections produce such leaders as well—sometimes precisely because inflammatory rhetoric and celebrity are electoral advantages. The relevant question is not whether sortition eliminates human weakness, but whether its risks are easier to control than those created by money-driven partisan competition.

A viable system would require:

  • large representative bodies rather than tiny samples;
  • stratified selection to prevent demographic distortion;
  • mandatory training and access to independent expertise;
  • fair compensation and employment protection;
  • transparent meetings and published evidence;
  • strict anti-bribery and conflict-of-interest rules;
  • short, staggered, nonrenewable terms;
  • collective rather than personal executive power;
  • independent courts and auditors;
  • procedures for incapacity, misconduct, and emergency review; and
  • constitutional protection for civil rights and minority liberties.

These safeguards would preserve the benefits of randomness while limiting arbitrariness and abuse.

A More Democratic Conception of Citizenship

The deepest argument for sortition is philosophical. Elections encourage citizens to think of democracy primarily as choosing rulers. Sortition asks them to understand democracy as sharing the work of ruling.

That change would transform public life. Government would no longer appear to belong to distant professionals who speak in slogans and return every few years to request votes. It would become an institution populated by neighbors, coworkers, caregivers, and community members. Civic education would gain practical importance because anyone might be called to serve. Citizens could see themselves not merely as spectators or partisan consumers, but as potential lawmakers and public stewards.

Ancient democracies used selection by lot because they understood that elections often favor the wealthy, famous, and socially connected. The scale and complexity of the modern United States demand a far more sophisticated system, but the underlying principle remains compelling: if political equality is real, ordinary citizens must have an equal opportunity to wield public power.

Conclusion

The American electoral system does not merely suffer from bad candidates or excessive polarization. Its central incentives reward fundraising, ambition, branding, and partisan combat. Reforms such as campaign-finance limits, ranked-choice voting, and independent redistricting may reduce some harms, but they leave the permanent campaign—and the political class it creates—fundamentally intact.

Sortition offers a more radical and democratic alternative. By choosing legislative and executive leaders from the citizenry, the United States could sharply reduce donor influence, weaken partisan incentives, broaden representation, and make public office a shared civic responsibility. Combined with professional administration, rigorous training, transparency, judicial review, and strict ethics enforcement, random selection could produce government that is not only more representative but also more thoughtful and less corrupt.

Democracy should mean more than periodically selecting which elite will govern. It should mean that the people themselves—ordinary, diverse, imperfect, and collectively capable—take turns exercising power. Sortition would make that promise real.

The United States is a nation built on the principle that government derives its legitimacy from the people. A lobbyist cannot simply invest in the expectation of reaping electoral returns, because leadership is not a prize won through campaigning—it's a duty randomly assigned from the citizenry.

Partisanship thrives when political competition is permanent and personal. When elections determine who holds power, parties become engines of identity, mobilization, and conflict. This dynamic doesn’t merely reflect polarization; it manufactures it.

If legislative and executive leaders are selected by lottery, parties lose the central advantage of controlling who can realistically win office. Campaigning becomes less relevant, and therefore parties have less leverage as gatekeepers of power. Without the constant electoral battlefield:

  • The incentive to build a “brand” loyal to a faction weakens.
  • Governance becomes less about outbidding rivals and more about solving problems.

Party affiliation can still exist, but it no longer functions as the direct ladder to authority. Instead of polarization being rewarded by electoral success, it becomes just one opinion among many—checked by deliberation, oversight, and rotation.

It means the leadership body becomes representative of the public’s diversity of views over time rather than a curated subset from party pipelines. A legislature composed of randomly selected citizens, rotated periodically, is far less likely to become an echo chamber of one faction’s priorities.

Democracy is not merely voting; it is also having a meaningful role in governing. Elections invite citizens to participate episodically, often indirectly, through selecting among professional candidates. Many citizens feel their choices are constrained: candidates reflect donors’ influence, media incentives, and party strategies more than the lived realities of everyday Americans.

Sortition offers something fundamentally different: it turns democracy from spectator participation into shared civic responsibility.

  • Government stops being something “done to” citizens and becomes something citizens actively do.
  • The barrier to representation falls dramatically. People who would never win elections due to lack of resources, network ties, or campaign readiness can still serve.

Even when disagreement persists, the sense that decisions were made by fellow citizens—not distant elites—reduces alienation and resentment.

Elections in the United States have always been a tool for democratic selection, but they have evolved into a system that rewards money, entrenches party dominance, and encourages corruption through predictable incentives. The result is a political environment in which the public often feels excluded, and where governance can drift toward the interests of those who fund and influence political careers.

Sortition offers a democratic corrective: replace electoral selection for legislative and executive leaders with random selection of qualified citizens, supported by transparency, training, expert advisory structures, and strong ethics enforcement. This approach can:

  • diminish partisanship by weakening party gatekeeping and career incentives,

Democracy Reimagined: How Sortition Can Rescue America from Political Corruption

The American experiment in democracy stands at a crossroads. Our electoral system, once hailed as a beacon of representative government, has devolved into a cesspool of corruption, partisan warfare, and elite capture. Billionaires buy influence, corporations write legislation, and career politicians serve party interests over public welfare. It's time to admit that elections—the foundation of our democratic system—have become the problem rather than the solution. The answer lies not in reforming our broken electoral process, but in replacing it entirely with sortition: government by random selection of citizens.

The Corruption Crisis: Why Elections Fail Us

Our current system creates an inherently corrupt dynamic. Politicians must constantly fundraise to win elections, making them beholden to wealthy donors rather than ordinary constituents. The revolving door between government service and lucrative lobbying positions ensures that public officials often serve corporate interests even while in office. This isn't a bug in the system—it's a feature of any system where political power is purchased through campaigns.

Consider the staggering numbers: members of Congress spend 30-70% of their time fundraising, time that should be devoted to governing. The average winning Senate campaign costs over $10 million, while House races regularly exceed $2 million. These astronomical sums don't come from small donations by ordinary citizens; they come from PACs, Super PACs, and wealthy individuals with specific policy agendas.

Sortition eliminates this fundamental corruption by removing money from the equation entirely. When citizens are selected randomly to serve, there are no campaigns to finance, no donors to please, and no electoral obligations to powerful interests. Selected representatives serve their full terms knowing they will return to civilian life afterward, removing the career incentive that drives so much political corruption.

Breaking the Partisan Death Spiral

American politics has become a tribal warfare where party loyalty trumps policy effectiveness and national interest. Elected officials face intense pressure from primary challengers who can defeat them by attacking them from the extreme ends of their party spectrum. This creates a system where moderate, pragmatic solutions become political suicide, and polarization escalates with each election cycle.

Sortition offers a powerful antidote to this destructive dynamic. Randomly selected citizens don't arrive with pre-packaged ideological positions or party loyalty oaths. They bring diverse perspectives shaped by their actual life experiences rather than cable news echo chambers. Studies of citizens' assemblies around the world demonstrate that when ordinary people deliberate together on complex issues, they consistently move toward more nuanced, evidence-based positions rather than rigid ideological stances.

Without the pressure to win re-election or satisfy party bosses, sortition-selected legislators could tackle difficult problems pragmatically. Climate change, healthcare reform, infrastructure investment—these challenges require long-term thinking that current electoral pressures make nearly impossible. Sortition would create space for the collaborative problem-solving our nation desperately needs.

Power to the People: Restoring True Representation

The promise of American democracy has always been rule by the people, yet our current system represents primarily those with the resources to influence elections. Wealthy Americans have disproportionate political power, while low-income citizens, racial minorities, and young people remain systematically underrepresented. The result is policy that favors the affluent while leaving working families behind.

Sortition democratizes representation in the most literal sense. Every citizen has an equal chance of being selected for service, ensuring that government truly reflects the population's diversity. When the farmer in Iowa, the teacher in Detroit, and the nurse in Phoenix have the same opportunity to shape national policy as billionaires and corporate executives, we begin to realize the egalitarian vision of our founding documents.

Moreover, sortition-selected bodies would bring authentic expertise to governance. Current legislators often lack direct experience with the challenges facing ordinary Americans. Teachers understand education problems from both instruction and parenting perspectives. Small business owners grasp regulatory challenges intimately. Healthcare workers know the system's failures firsthand. Random selection ensures that people with real-world knowledge participate in creating policies that affect their daily lives.

Practical Implementation: A Path Forward

Critics argue that sortition sounds radical, but aspects of this system already exist successfully. Jury duty demonstrates how random selection can identify trustworthy citizens willing to serve their communities. Many organizations use random sampling for decision-making bodies. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly proved that sortition-based bodies can tackle complex constitutional issues thoughtfully and effectively.

A transitional approach could begin with establishing citizen assemblies at state and local levels to address specific policy challenges. These bodies would demonstrate sortition's effectiveness while building public confidence in the process. Gradually, we could expand citizen selection to more governmental functions, eventually transitioning to a primarily sortition-based system for most legislative and executive positions.

The technology already exists to make sortition practical on a large scale. Modern databases and communication systems could randomly select representative samples of citizens while ensuring demographic balance. Remote participation technology could minimize disruption to citizens' lives while maximizing accessibility.

Addressing Legitimate Concerns

Skeptics raise valid questions about qualifications and accountability. However, sortition doesn't eliminate all training or preparation. Selected citizens would undergo orientation programs similar to those provided to newly elected officials. Additionally, sortition bodies could establish mentorship programs pairing new members with experienced advisors during their service terms.

Regarding expertise, sortition actually enhances collective wisdom by bringing diverse knowledge and perspectives together. No single elected official can match the combined experience of a randomly selected group representing various professions, ages, and backgrounds. Furthermore, sortition-selected bodies would have access to expert testimony, research, and consultation just as current legislatures do.

Term limits addressed through sortition's inherent rotation system ensure regular influx of fresh perspectives while preventing the entrenched power dynamics that corrupt long-serving elected officials.

The Moral Imperative

At its core, this debate isn't just about governance efficiency—it's about justice and democratic legitimacy. When political power consolidates among wealthy elites and career politicians, we betray the fundamental principle that government should serve all citizens equally. Sortition offers a path back to genuinely popular rule, where ordinary people exercise direct control over their collective destiny.

The American founders themselves worried about the corrupting influence of electoral politics. James Madison wrote extensively about factions and the dangers of organized interests dominating government. They created systems of checks and balances to limit these dangers, but none anticipated how completely money would come to dominate elections or how thoroughly partisan tribalism would replace principled governance.

Sortition represents a return to the founders' deepest democratic intuitions while adapting to modern realities. It harnesses the wisdom of crowds, the diversity of perspectives, and the legitimate authority of popular consent in ways that our current system simply cannot achieve.

Conclusion: Embracing Democratic Innovation

America's democratic institutions weren't handed down from heaven—they were created by human beings solving human problems. When those solutions stop working, we have both the right and responsibility to innovate. Sortition offers a proven alternative that eliminates the root causes of our political dysfunction while enhancing democratic participation and representation.

The choice before us is stark: continue with a system that produces predictable corruption, escalating polarization, and widespread citizen alienation—or embrace a bold innovation that puts power back where it belongs, in the hands of ordinary Americans selected fairly to serve their fellow citizens.

Sortition won't solve every problem overnight, but it addresses the fundamental structural flaws that plague our current system. By removing elections, we remove the primary mechanisms through which special interests capture government, parties enforce ideological conformity, and wealth translates into political power.

The question isn't whether sortition is perfect—it's whether it's better than what we have now. Given the urgent challenges facing our nation and the demonstrable failures of electoral politics to address them effectively, sortition represents not just an alternative, but a necessity for restoring healthy democratic governance in America.

The time for half-measures and incremental reform has passed. We must dare to reimagine democracy itself, embracing sortition as the tool that will finally make government truly of the people, by the people, and for the people.

In the United States, the current election system is riddled with political corruption, partisanship, and a disconnection between ordinary citizens and the political process. The dominant influence of donors, special interests, and party machinery has eroded accountability, fostered gridlock, and undermined the legitimacy of elected officials. The current electoral system is a bastion of cronyism, where wealthy donors, lobbyists, and corporations dictate policy outcomes. Sortition eliminates this by ensuring representatives are chosen randomly from the citizenry, not based on financial or ideological connections. This shift would:

  • Level the Playing Field: Without the influence of big money, ordinary citizens would have a direct, equal voice in selecting leaders, reducing the corrosive effect of corruption that has tainted policy-making for decades. For example, in 2010, the Supreme Court ruled that the First Amendment allows corporations to spend millions of dollars to influence elections, further entrenching the status quo.

Term limits, recall mechanisms, and public opinion polls would further safeguard against corruption and ensure elected officials remain accountable to the broader citizenry.

The hyper-partisan nature of American politics—rooted in gerrymandering, safe-seat strategies, and donor-driven campaigns—creates a toxic political environment. Sortition would diversify representation, potentially bridging party lines and fostering cooperation. Key benefits include:

  • Diverse Representation: Random selection would ensure a broader demographic and ideological representation, reducing the dominance of two parties and allowing for more balanced policy discussions. This could lead to legislation that addresses pressing national issues more effectively, such as climate change or healthcare reform.

  • Cross-Party Collaboration: With a more representative legislature, elected officials from different parties would be incentivized to work together on common goals, breaking the partisan stalemate that has stalled progress on critical issues.   • Legislative Efficiency: A randomized system would reduce the reliance on partisan ideology, as representatives would be selected based on merit, not political affiliation. This could lead to more pragmatic, consensus-driven policies, as seen in the bipartisan compromise on tax reform in 2017.

3. Empowering Ordinary Citizens

The current system often feels disconnected for ordinary people, as elections are dominated by donors and special interests. Sortition empowers citizens by giving them a direct role in selecting leaders, making them the primary influencers in policy-making. Key benefits include:

The current electoral system is a relic of 19th-century politics, designed to protect the interests of the wealthy and the powerful. Sortition is the ultimate fairness. It acknowledges that no one citizen is intrinsically "better" than another. It asserts that the single mother understanding the price of milk is just as vital to our leadership as the economist who tracks the price of gold.

It is time to take the consistent, corruption-proof gamble on the American people.

Let us tear down the stages, return the campaign donations, fire the consultants, and silence the spin doctors. Let us hand the gavel to the people—the real people.

This is not anarchy. This is maturity. This is the realization that power corrupts, so power must be rotated, random, and rooted in the soil of the common citizen.

Let us be brave enough to admit the experiment of career politics has failed. Let us be bold enough to trust one another.

Abolish elections. Install the lottery. And finally, for the first time in our history, let us have a government that is truly, undeniably, of the people, by the people, and for the people.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of replacing all elections in the United States with a system of sortition, where legislative and executive leaders are chosen through random citizen selection, emphasizing how this approach removes political corruption, reduces partisanship, and empowers ordinary people.
Model Response:

Why the United States Should Replace Elections with Sortition

For generations, Americans have been taught to treat elections as the heart of democracy. Voting is presented as the ultimate expression of popular rule, and elections are often described as the only legitimate way to choose leaders. But this assumption deserves far more scrutiny than it usually receives. In practice, modern elections in the United States have become engines of corruption, polarization, and alienation. They reward wealth, celebrity, manipulation, and tribal loyalty far more than wisdom, integrity, or public service. Instead of empowering ordinary citizens, elections have created a professional political class that governs over the public rather than with it.

A better alternative exists: sortition, the selection of political leaders through random citizen choice. Under sortition, legislative and executive roles would be filled by ordinary Americans chosen much like jurors are chosen today. With proper safeguards, training, term limits, and expert support, this system would produce a government that is more representative, less corrupt, less partisan, and far more democratic in substance than the current electoral model. If the United States is serious about self-government, it should replace elections with sortition.

Elections Do Not Give Power to the People

The central myth of electoral democracy is that elections empower citizens. In reality, they mostly empower the tiny fraction of citizens who have the money, connections, ambition, and social advantages needed to compete for office. Most Americans will never run for Congress, never be governor, never seriously contend for the presidency, and never have any realistic chance of shaping national policy directly. Their role is reduced to choosing between pre-packaged candidates who have already survived donor screening, party gatekeeping, media filtering, and campaign warfare.

This is not genuine popular rule. It is a narrow competition among elites for permission to govern.

Sortition changes that completely. It says that public office should not be reserved for the rich, the famous, the ruthless, or the professionally ambitious. It should be open to everyone. A teacher, mechanic, nurse, warehouse worker, retiree, parent, or student should be just as likely to help govern the country as a millionaire lawyer or media-trained partisan operative. Random selection would make political power something that can genuinely belong to the people as a whole, not just to those who can win campaigns.

That is a far deeper form of democracy than voting every few years for candidates manufactured by parties and donors.

Sortition Would Strike at the Root of Political Corruption

One of the strongest arguments for replacing elections is that elections create corruption by design. Candidates need money to run. They need donors, fundraisers, consultants, advertising, party support, and favorable media coverage. Even when politicians are not literally bribed, they are constantly shaped by the interests of those who finance their careers. They learn quickly whose calls to return, whose concerns to prioritize, and whose anger to fear. The result is a government that is formally elected by the public but functionally dependent on wealthy backers and organized interests.

Sortition breaks this relationship.

A randomly selected citizen does not need to raise millions of dollars. They do not need lobbyist money, corporate PACs, billionaire patrons, or party machinery. They do not need to spend years flattering donors or making policy promises tailored to campaign contributors. Because they are not chosen through fundraising, they cannot be controlled through fundraising. Because they do not need reelection, they are far less vulnerable to pressure from interest groups and polling swings.

This would remove one of the greatest sources of corruption in American political life: the permanent campaign.

Under sortition, there would be no incentive to buy political influence by bankrolling candidates. There would be no campaign war chest to build, no electoral machine to feed, and no reelection strategy to manipulate. Lobbyists would lose one of their most powerful tools, because randomly selected officials would not owe their positions to anyone except chance and citizenship. That alone would dramatically reduce the power of money in politics.

Critics may object that ordinary citizens could still be influenced once in office. Of course they could. No system can eliminate all bad behavior. But sortition would eliminate the institutional pipeline that currently makes corruption routine. It is much harder to systematically corrupt a rotating, randomly chosen citizen body than a stable class of career politicians whose ambitions, networks, and vulnerabilities are all publicly known and continuously exploitable.

Elections Intensify Partisanship; Sortition Would Cool It Down

Another devastating problem with elections is that they reward division. Candidates do not win by bringing everyone together. They win by mobilizing their side, demonizing opponents, simplifying complex issues into slogans, and inflaming cultural resentment. Electoral politics turns every disagreement into a battle for total victory. It pushes citizens into rigid camps and trains politicians to treat compromise as weakness.

This is why American politics feels less like democratic deliberation and more like perpetual warfare.

Sortition offers a radically healthier alternative. Randomly selected citizens would not enter office as professional partisans. They would not need to perform outrage for television clips, appeal to a primary electorate, or obsess over campaign messaging. They would not spend years cultivating ideological brands. Instead, they would arrive as ordinary people with mixed experiences, complicated beliefs, and far less incentive to view politics as tribal combat.

That matters immensely.

When people are not forced to campaign, they can deliberate. When they are not trying to win elections, they can listen. When they do not need to satisfy party activists or donor networks, they can change their minds. Sortition creates the conditions for politics to become a process of shared problem-solving instead of endless partisan theater.

Evidence from citizens' assemblies and deliberative bodies around the world supports this idea. When ordinary people are randomly selected, given time, balanced information, and serious responsibility, they often become more thoughtful, more open-minded, and more capable of compromise than professional politicians. They are not magically wiser than elected officials in every case, but they are often far less trapped by ideological performance and partisan incentives.

In short, elections create polarization because they reward it. Sortition would reduce polarization because it makes cooperation more useful than conflict.

Ordinary Citizens Are More Than Capable of Governing

A common objection to sortition is that average people are not qualified to lead. But this objection reveals a profound and anti-democratic prejudice. Ordinary Americans already make life-and-death decisions as parents, workers, soldiers, nurses, engineers, judges, teachers, and jurors. Juries, in particular, are trusted to weigh evidence, determine facts, and decide guilt or innocence in serious criminal trials. If citizens are competent enough to decide whether someone loses their liberty, they are competent enough to help decide tax policy, infrastructure priorities, education reform, or healthcare legislation.

The real issue is not whether ordinary people are inherently incapable. It is whether they are given the support needed to govern well.

Under a sortition system, they would be. Randomly selected leaders could receive extensive briefings, access to independent experts, nonpartisan staff support, ethics oversight, and structured deliberation. Just as jurors are guided through legal processes, citizen-legislators and citizen-executives could be guided through governance. Competence is not something only politicians possess; it is something institutions can cultivate.

Indeed, career politicians often display the opposite of competence. They may be skilled at campaigning, fundraising, debating, or media management, but those are not the same as governing wisely. Winning elections selects for ambition, charisma, and manipulation—not necessarily judgment, honesty, or practical wisdom. Sortition, by contrast, would produce leaders who more closely resemble the public and who are far more likely to bring real-world experience into government.

A legislature filled with ordinary citizens would include people who have actually dealt with public schools, hospitals, rent, childcare, shift work, elder care, military service, disability, commuting, and local community problems. That kind of lived knowledge is badly missing from American political institutions. Sortition would restore it.

Sortition Would Create a Government That Looks Like America

Elections produce distortion. Wealthy candidates are overrepresented. Lawyers are overrepresented. career partisans are overrepresented. Meanwhile, working-class people, caregivers, young adults, the poor, and many others remain deeply underrepresented. Even when elected bodies contain some diversity, they still tend to share a common social profile: highly educated, professionally political, and separated from everyday life.

Sortition would create a government that actually mirrors the population.

A random selection system can be designed to ensure demographic fairness across region, age, race, gender, class, and other factors. The result would be a governing body that is not merely symbolic of the public but genuinely composed of it. Citizens would no longer look at government and see a distant ruling class. They would see themselves, their neighbors, and people with experiences like their own.

This matters for legitimacy. People are more likely to trust institutions that feel accessible and representative. When office becomes something any citizen could be called to serve in, politics stops being a spectator sport and becomes a shared civic duty. That is profoundly empowering.

Instead of asking citizens to occasionally endorse elites, sortition invites citizens to directly participate in ruling. It transforms democracy from passive selection into active self-government.

Replacing Elections Would Revive Civic Responsibility

Modern electoral culture encourages cynicism. Millions of Americans feel that their vote barely matters, that candidates lie, that parties are corrupt, and that government is controlled by forces beyond public reach. This alienation is not irrational; it is the natural response to a system in which ordinary people have almost no direct role.

Sortition would revive civic life by making public service real and immediate. Just as jury duty reminds people that justice belongs to the citizenry, sortition would remind Americans that government belongs to them. Citizens would not just be asked to complain, donate, vote, and watch. They would be asked to serve.

That expectation could transform the political culture of the country. People would have greater incentive to stay informed, to think seriously about public issues, and to understand the responsibilities of governance. Politics would no longer be monopolized by professionals and commentators. It would become a normal part of citizenship.

This is one of the most powerful moral arguments for sortition: it treats ordinary people as adults capable of self-rule. Elections flatter the public rhetorically while excluding it practically. Sortition respects the public enough to hand it the reins.

The Executive Should Also Be Chosen by Sortition

Some may accept sortition for legislatures but hesitate when it comes to executive leadership. Yet the modern presidency has become one of the clearest examples of the failures of elections. Presidential campaigns are spectacles of branding, donor influence, media manipulation, and personality cults. They reward theatrical confidence, not steady judgment. They turn national leadership into a popularity contest distorted by money and mass persuasion.

A randomly selected executive, especially one serving a fixed term with advisory councils and strong institutional checks, would be less likely to govern as a partisan celebrity. Such a leader would not owe power to a political machine or electoral base. They would enter office with a duty to the whole public, not to the coalition that delivered victory. While they would still need expert support and constitutional constraints, they would be freer to govern pragmatically and honestly.

Most importantly, choosing the executive by lot would deprive the office of the quasi-monarchical aura that electoral spectacle has created. The president would no longer be treated as a savior, champion, or tribal symbol. The office would become what it should be: a public role temporarily held by a citizen in service to the republic.

Conclusion

The United States should replace elections with sortition because elections have failed on their own democratic promises. They do not truly empower the people; they elevate elites. They do not eliminate corruption; they institutionalize dependence on money and influence. They do not foster unity; they deepen partisanship and turn politics into permanent conflict. They do not reliably select the wisest leaders; they select the best campaigners.

Sortition offers a bold but superior alternative. By choosing leaders randomly from the citizenry, America could build a government that is more representative, less corrupt, less partisan, and more faithful to the principle of self-rule. It would break the grip of donors and parties, reduce ideological warfare, and place ordinary people at the center of public power where they belong.

Democracy should mean more than choosing which elite gets to rule. It should mean that the people truly govern themselves. Sortition is the system most capable of making that promise real.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a nationwide system of sortition—random lottery selection of legislative and executive leaders—instead of using traditional elections, focusing on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.
Model Response:

Supporters of sortition argue that replacing elections with some form of random lottery selection for lawmakers—and in some versions even for executive leaders—could make government fairer, less dominated by elites, and more genuinely representative of the public.

The basic idea is simple: instead of asking citizens to compete for office through campaigns, fundraising, party backing, and media performance, the state would randomly select ordinary citizens from the population, much like jury duty, to serve for a limited term.

Here are the main claimed benefits.

1. It could make political power more equal

In elections, not everyone has a realistic chance of holding office. In practice, people are far more likely to win if they have:

  • money
  • social connections
  • party support
  • high name recognition
  • media skills
  • elite educational credentials
  • time and resources to campaign

Sortition changes the principle of access to power. Instead of “the most competitive win,” it becomes “every citizen has an equal chance to serve.”

Advocates say this is fairer because:

  • political office stops being a prize for the well-connected
  • ordinary citizens become actual participants in governing
  • power is not filtered through campaign machinery
  • citizens are treated more like political equals, not just voters choosing among elites

So from a fairness perspective, sortition is attractive because it gives equal opportunity to govern, not merely equal opportunity to cast a ballot.

2. It could sharply reduce elite influence

One of the strongest arguments for sortition is that elections tend to produce a self-reinforcing political class.

Traditional elections often favor people who can:

  • raise large sums of money
  • appeal to donors
  • secure endorsements
  • work party networks
  • attract media attention
  • build long-term political careers

This creates a system in which major decisions are often shaped by:

  • wealthy donors
  • lobbyists
  • party insiders
  • consultants
  • interest groups
  • corporations and major media institutions

Sortition weakens those pathways.

Why?

Because randomly selected leaders do not need to campaign, and if they do not need to campaign, they do not need:

  • donor money
  • political branding
  • party loyalty
  • celebrity status
  • professional campaign staffs

That means many of the usual ways elites influence politics become less effective.

Advocates argue that this would:

  • reduce corruption tied to campaign finance
  • reduce policymaking shaped by donors rather than citizens
  • limit the rise of permanent political insiders
  • make lobbying less predictable and less profitable
  • prevent powerful groups from grooming favored candidates years in advance

In short, sortition aims to break the pipeline by which wealth and institutional power convert into political control.

3. It could create a legislature that actually looks like the country

Elected bodies are often not representative in any descriptive sense. They tend to overrepresent:

  • the wealthy
  • highly educated professionals
  • older people
  • men
  • urban elites or party loyalists
  • people with unusual ambition and thick skin for public combat

They tend to underrepresent:

  • working-class citizens
  • caregivers
  • people with disabilities
  • racial, ethnic, and religious minorities
  • people from less prestigious backgrounds
  • citizens who are thoughtful but not performative
  • people who do not want a political career

A well-designed sortition system could produce an assembly that more closely mirrors the real population in terms of:

  • age
  • gender
  • income
  • region
  • ethnicity
  • occupation
  • education
  • life experience

This is one of the most important democratic arguments for sortition: instead of being represented by a small political elite, citizens would be represented by a microcosm of themselves.

Advocates say that this can improve legitimacy because people may feel:

  • “people like me are actually in the room”
  • “government is no longer something done by a separate caste”
  • “public decisions are being made by society itself, not by professionals alone”

4. It may select for ordinary judgment rather than campaign skill

Elections often reward qualities that are useful for winning elections, not necessarily for governing well.

For example, elected officials often need to be good at:

  • self-promotion
  • attacking opponents
  • simplifying complex issues into slogans
  • performing in media environments
  • constant fundraising
  • partisan messaging

But those are not always the same traits needed for sound public judgment.

Sortition supporters argue that random selection is better because it does not systematically favor people who are:

  • charismatic
  • wealthy
  • manipulative
  • ambitious for power
  • unusually good at political theater

Instead, it opens the door for citizens who may be:

  • practical
  • level-headed
  • community-minded
  • less ideological
  • more open to evidence
  • more reflective than performative

The claim is not that every randomly selected citizen would be excellent. It is that, on average, a properly supported group of ordinary citizens may exercise more authentic civic judgment than a class of people selected primarily for their ability to win campaigns.

5. It could reduce polarization and partisan warfare

Elections create strong incentives for division:

  • candidates must distinguish themselves from rivals
  • parties benefit from mobilizing anger and fear
  • media rewards conflict
  • reelection encourages constant positioning against opponents

As a result, electoral politics often becomes theatrical, tribal, and zero-sum.

Sortition could reduce this because randomly selected officials would not necessarily owe loyalty to:

  • a party machine
  • a donor coalition
  • an activist base
  • a campaign narrative

Without the need to win the next election, they may be more willing to:

  • listen to opposing views
  • revise their opinions
  • compromise
  • deliberate rather than posture
  • think about long-term outcomes

Advocates often point to citizens’ assemblies and jury-style processes, where ordinary people, given time and information, often become less extreme and more thoughtful than the general political climate.

So the claim is that sortition could produce a calmer form of democracy centered on deliberation instead of permanent campaigning.

6. It could improve deliberation and decision quality

Sortition systems are usually not imagined as “pick random people and give them no help.” Proponents usually pair sortition with:

  • expert briefings
  • balanced evidence packets
  • hearings
  • moderated discussion
  • access to civil servants and policy experts
  • time to learn before deciding

Under those conditions, advocates argue, citizens can make serious decisions surprisingly well.

Why might this work better than electoral politics?

Because elected officials often have distorted incentives:

  • they must think about reelection
  • they fear media backlash
  • they cater to partisan audiences
  • they avoid complex but necessary tradeoffs
  • they often speak for supporters rather than consider the whole

A sortition-based body may be freer to ask:

  • What is true?
  • What is fair?
  • What works?
  • What tradeoffs are acceptable for society as a whole?

The argument is that randomly selected citizens, when given structure and information, can act as a deliberative public, rather than as partisan competitors.

7. It could reduce corruption and careerism

When political office becomes a career, officeholders can begin making decisions not for the public good but for:

  • reelection
  • future lobbying jobs
  • party advancement
  • media opportunities
  • donor relationships
  • factional power

Sortition disrupts that model.

If service is:

  • temporary
  • randomly assigned
  • difficult to predict
  • not easily repeated

then it becomes much harder to build a permanent power base.

Supporters say this reduces:

  • entrenched patronage networks
  • long-term quid pro quo relationships
  • dynastic politics
  • the revolving door between office and influence industries
  • strategic ambition as the main path into leadership

Instead of officeholders seeing themselves as political entrepreneurs, they may see themselves more as temporary civic trustees.

8. It could better include marginalized voices

Election systems often silence or exclude people who lack time, money, confidence, or institutional support. Many people who are capable of making valuable political contributions never run for office because they are:

  • too busy working or caregiving
  • uninterested in public self-exposure
  • discouraged by party gatekeepers
  • unable to afford campaigning
  • alienated from political culture

Sortition can include such people by making public service a shared civic obligation and opportunity, not a competitive market.

With proper accommodations—such as salary, childcare, translation, disability access, job protection, and training—a sortition system could bring in people whose experiences are rarely reflected in elected government.

Advocates see this as a major democratic gain: politics becomes less about who can survive elite institutions and more about drawing on the full social intelligence of the population.

9. It changes democracy from “choosing rulers” to “sharing rule”

A deeper philosophical argument is that elections are only partly democratic.

In this view, elections let citizens choose among elites, but they do not let the public directly participate in governing. Over time, this can create a gap between “the people” and “the state.”

Sortition narrows that gap.

Its supporters say true democracy should not mean merely:

  • voting every few years
  • watching professionals govern
  • hoping representatives keep promises

It should mean that citizens themselves take turns exercising power.

Under this ideal, sortition turns democracy into something closer to:

  • collective self-government
  • civic rotation
  • public service distributed across the population
  • political equality in practice, not just in theory

This is one reason sortition is often described as more democratic in spirit than elections: it treats citizens not only as choosers, but as potential governors.

10. Why some proponents extend sortition to executive leadership

Using sortition for a legislature is easier to imagine than using it for presidents or prime ministers. Still, some advocates argue executive power should also be selected by lottery, or at least partly so.

Their reasons include:

A. It reduces personality cults

Executive elections often revolve around charismatic individuals, which can encourage:

  • demagoguery
  • emotional mass politics
  • celebrity leadership
  • authoritarian tendencies

Random selection could weaken the idea that the nation needs a heroic figure.

B. It prevents concentration of ambition

People most eager for top executive office are not always the most trustworthy. Sortition reduces the advantage of those who are obsessed with power.

C. It weakens national-level oligarchic capture

Executive elections are expensive and highly vulnerable to manipulation by donors, media systems, and party elites. A lottery-based process would be harder to dominate through those channels.

D. It encourages collective or council-based executive models

Rather than one powerful elected leader, a sortition system might use:

  • a randomly selected executive council
  • rotating chairs
  • mixed bodies of citizens and experts
  • officials chosen by lot from a qualified public pool

Proponents say this can make executive power more restrained, less personalized, and less susceptible to authoritarian drift.

That said, even many supporters of sortition prefer applying it more heavily to legislatures, oversight bodies, and constitutional conventions than to a single all-powerful executive office.

11. It may increase trust and legitimacy

Many people feel current democracies are controlled by:

  • political insiders
  • donors
  • bureaucratic elites
  • media narratives
  • party establishments

Sortition offers a different source of legitimacy: the government is legitimate because it is literally made up of the people in miniature.

Supporters argue that this may increase trust because:

  • the selection process is simple and transparent
  • no one “buys” their way in
  • no faction fully owns the institutions
  • decisions come from a body that resembles society
  • citizens know they themselves might someday serve

This kind of legitimacy is less about electoral victory and more about fair inclusion.

12. A concise summary of the case for sortition

Advocates think nationwide sortition could improve government because it would:

  • give all citizens a more equal chance to hold power
  • reduce the role of money, parties, and media manipulation
  • weaken entrenched elites and career politicians
  • create assemblies that mirror the actual population
  • include voices normally shut out of office
  • reduce polarization and constant campaigning
  • encourage more thoughtful deliberation
  • limit corruption tied to reelection and donor dependence
  • make democracy feel like shared rule, not elite competition

Important caveat

These are the supposed benefits claimed by supporters. Critics raise major concerns too, such as:

  • competence
  • accountability
  • continuity
  • public consent
  • vulnerability to manipulation by unelected experts or bureaucrats

So in practice, many real-world proponents favor mixed systems rather than abolishing elections entirely—for example, combining elected institutions with randomly selected citizens’ chambers or assemblies.

But if you want the strongest case for sortition, it is this:

elections tend to select ambitious, well-funded, well-connected elites, while sortition aims to distribute political power broadly across ordinary citizens, making government fairer, less oligarchic, and more representative of society as a whole.

If you want, I can also provide:

  1. a comparison table of elections vs. sortition, or
  2. the strongest criticisms of sortition.
